body: What is the major objective of teaching? To

options.text: bring about a change in the individual
options.hint: Correct. Teaching aims at desirable behaviour change.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Teaching is planned activity aimed at producing **desirable, relatively permanent change** in learners' knowledge, skills and attitudes.

## Simplified explanation

Change in the learner.

body: One of the major characteristics of a scientific discipline such as psychology is its ability to
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The goals of psychology as a science are to **describe, explain, predict and control** behaviour.

## Simplified explanation

Predict and control.

body: A successful teacher is identified by a large store of teaching skills and knowledge in

options.hint: Correct. Mastery of content plus teaching skills.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Effective teaching combines an **action system** (teaching skills) with **subject-matter knowledge**.

## Simplified explanation

Content mastery.

body: Having a large store of teaching skills is referred to as

options.hint: Correct. The teacher's repertoire of skills.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Teaching as an art involves **action system knowledge** (a store of teaching skills), subject-matter knowledge, communication skills and personality.

## Simplified explanation

Action system knowledge.

body: Which of the following does **not** come to the fore when explaining teaching as an **art**?

options.text: Mastery of the action system and subject-matter knowledge

options.hint: Correct. A positive personality is required.

options.text: Materials teachers use to present learning activities

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Teaching as an art draws on skill, creativity, communication and a **positive** personality.

## Simplified explanation

Not *negative* personality.

body: The two ways in which instruction can be perceived are as a system and as a
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Instruction can be viewed as a **system** (interrelated parts) or a **process** (the way the teacher imparts knowledge).

## Simplified explanation

**Process**.

body: The way or strategy through which the instructor imparts knowledge to the learner is referred to as instruction as a
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Instruction-as-process = the **methods/strategies** of delivery.

## Simplified explanation

**Process**.

body: What is the main difference between instructional objectives and educational objectives? Instructional objectives are

options.text: more specific and immediate than educational objectives

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Educational objectives** are broad, long-term goals; **instructional objectives** are specific, measurable, short-term lesson outcomes.

## Simplified explanation

Specific and immediate.

body: Sternberg (1981) defined intelligence as the ability to learn, adjust to the environment, adapt to new situations or
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Intelligence definitions stress learning, adaptation and the ability to **profit from experience**.

## Simplified explanation

Profit from experience.

body: Which of the following is **not** one of Erikson's stages of psychosocial development?

options.hint: Correct. It's intimacy vs isolation; generativity vs stagnation.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Erikson's 8 stages: trust–mistrust, autonomy–shame, initiative–guilt, industry–inferiority, identity–role confusion, **intimacy–isolation**, **generativity–stagnation**, integrity–despair.

## Simplified explanation

Mismatched pair.

body: The relationship between parental resources, family size and academic performance is explained by

options.hint: Correct. Resources spread thinner as family size grows.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Blake's **resource dilution** model: parental time, money and attention are divided among more children, lowering each child's achievement.

## Simplified explanation

**Resource dilution**.

body: Which of the following is **not** one of the ways to help pupils develop **self-control**?

options.hint: Correct. Not one of Redl & Wattenberg's techniques.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Redl & Wattenberg's influence techniques for supporting self-control include **signal interference**, **proximity control**, **interest boosting**, humour and tension decontamination.

## Simplified explanation

Not 'speech control'.

body: Which of the following is **not** an example of positive reinforcement?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Positive reinforcement **adds** something pleasant after a behaviour to increase it; a rebuke is an aversive consequence intended to decrease it.

## Simplified explanation

**Rebuke** punishes.

body: Which of the following is **not** one of the four phases of observational learning?

options.hint: Correct. Not one of Bandura's phases.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bandura: **attention → retention → (motor) reproduction → motivation/reinforcement**.

## Simplified explanation

No 'forgetting' phase.

body: Which of the following psychologists is **not** associated with Gestalt theory?

options.hint: Correct. Confuses Max Wertheimer and Wolfgang Köhler.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Gestalt founders: **Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Köhler**: the whole is more than the sum of its parts; insight learning.

## Simplified explanation

No 'Max Kohler'.

body: What is the major advantage of the **circle** arrangement of classroom space?

options.text: The teacher is sure of good class control

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Circles promote **discussion and participation**; rows-and-columns suit teacher-centred instruction and control.

## Simplified explanation

Participation.

body: Which model of classroom management recommends **minimal teacher intervention**?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Wolfgang & Glickman continuum: **non-interventionist (humanistic)**, interactionist (democratic), interventionist (behaviourist).

## Simplified explanation

**Humanistic**.

body: Why should a teacher turn on their 'radar' (withitness) when teaching?

options.text: In order to see everybody in the class
To watch out for students whose attention is drifting
Because the teacher is the manager of the class
So that all the pupils can see the teacher

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Kounin's **withitness**: the teacher is aware of everything happening and catches inattention/misbehaviour early.

## Simplified explanation

Spot drifting attention.

body: Learning may be explained as a process whereby an organism changes its behaviour as a result of

options.hint: Correct. Relatively permanent change through experience.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Learning = a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to **experience or practice** (not maturation, fatigue or drugs).

## Simplified explanation

**Experience**.

body: Behaviour that is **emitted** by an organism as it interacts with the stimulus situation is associated with
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Skinner: **operant** behaviour is *emitted* and shaped by consequences; classical (respondent) behaviour is *elicited* by stimuli.

## Simplified explanation

Emitted = **operant**.

body: The process through which a conditioned stimulus gradually loses the ability to evoke a response when no longer followed by the unconditioned stimulus is

options.hint: Return of the CR after rest.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **extinction** the CS is presented repeatedly without the UCS, so the CR weakens.

## Simplified explanation

**Extinction**.

body: A situation where a stimulus is made to elicit a response that was not at first associated with it is known as
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Pavlov: pairing the bell (NS) with food (UCS) makes the bell alone elicit salivation (CR).

## Simplified explanation

**Classical conditioning**.

body: Which of the following is **not** one of the main concerns of Thorndike's instrumental conditioning theory?

options.text: The connection between stimulus and response

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Thorndike's connectionism: trial and error, S–R bonds and the laws of **effect, exercise and readiness**.

## Simplified explanation

Not 'terminal behaviour'.

body: The group of psychologists who focus on **overt** behaviour are called
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Behaviourists (Watson, Pavlov, Skinner, Thorndike) study observable behaviour.

## Simplified explanation

**Behaviourists**.

body: Through which medium does information enter our mind?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Information-processing: input enters through the **senses** into sensory memory, then STM and LTM.

## Simplified explanation

**Senses**.

body: Modelled activity is stored in long-term memory through verbal or visual codes and
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bandura's retention phase: symbolic **coding** (verbal/imaginal) plus **rehearsal**.

## Simplified explanation

**Rehearsal**.

body: Which part of the memory system stores large amounts of information for long periods of time?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

LTM has vast capacity and long duration; STM holds ~7±2 items for ~20 s.

## Simplified explanation

**LTM**.

body: Learning a list of terms in a particular order is
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Verbal learning types: **serial** (fixed order), **free recall** (any order), **paired-associate** (stimulus–response pairs).

## Simplified explanation

**Serial**.

body: Which motivational perspective is most concerned with the **personal development** of students?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Humanistic theorists stress growth, self-esteem and self-actualisation.

## Simplified explanation

**Humanistic**.

body: How did **instinct theory** describe motivation? As
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Instinct theory (McDougall) sees behaviour as driven by **innate, unlearned** tendencies.

## Simplified explanation

Unlearned.

body: **True or False?** Extrinsic motivation is less effective with younger pupils who are not impressed by the long-term value of the subject they study.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The opposite: young pupils who don't yet value long-term goals respond **well** to extrinsic rewards (praise, stars).

## Simplified explanation

Extrinsic works well for young learners.

body: **True or False?** Classroom environment has nothing to do with social and ecological systems.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The classroom environment includes physical (ecological) and social systems: relationships, climate, arrangement.

## Simplified explanation

It does.

body: **True or False?** According to advocates of the behavioural model of classroom management, behaviour is learned.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Behaviourists hold that behaviour (good or bad) is learned through reinforcement, so it can be reshaped.

## Simplified explanation

True.

body: Which location of the classroom is referred to as the **action zone**?

options.text: The front and centre of the classroom

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Adams & Biddle: pupils in the **front and centre** (T-shaped zone) interact most with the teacher.

## Simplified explanation

Front and centre.

body: The specialist who assesses and advises pupils about personal, academic and vocational problems is the
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Guidance counsellors handle **personal-social, educational and vocational** guidance.

## Simplified explanation

**Guidance counsellor**.

body: (a) Explain the term **educational psychology**. (b) State and explain **five** importances of educational psychology to you as a teacher.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** Educational psychology is the branch of psychology that applies **psychological principles, theories and research** to the study of **the learner, the learning process and the learning situation**, to improve teaching and learning.
>
> **(b)** It helps the teacher to: (1) understand **learners' developmental characteristics** and individual differences; (2) choose suitable **methods** based on learning theories; (3) **motivate** pupils; (4) **manage the classroom** effectively; (5) construct and use **assessment** properly; (6) identify and support learners with **special needs**; (7) formulate realistic **objectives**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Link each importance to a classroom example.

## Simplified explanation

Psychology applied to teaching; know your pupils, methods, motivation, management.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: (a) State and explain **three** theories of forgetting. (b) Describe techniques teachers can use to minimise forgetting in their pupils.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** (1) **Decay (trace) theory**: memory traces fade with disuse over time. (2) **Interference theory**: other learning disrupts recall: **proactive** (old blocks new) and **retroactive** (new blocks old). (3) **Motivated forgetting/repression** (Freud): painful memories are pushed out of awareness. (4) **Retrieval (cue-dependent) failure**: the information is stored but the cue to retrieve it is missing.
>
> **(b)** Regular **revision/spaced practice**; **overlearning**; making material **meaningful** and linked to prior knowledge; **mnemonics**; using multiple senses; **active recall** (quizzes); avoiding teaching similar topics back-to-back; giving adequate rest.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Pair each theory with a remedy.

## Simplified explanation

Fading, interference, repression, retrieval failure; revise and make meaningful.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: (a) Explain the **three** main models of classroom management. (b) Describe **five** procedures you consider an important basis for classroom management.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** (1) **Humanistic/non-interventionist**: pupils have inner drives to solve problems; teacher offers minimal intervention, empathy and support (Rogers, Gordon). (2) **Democratic/interactionist**: teacher and pupils share responsibility, setting rules together; high pupil participation (Dreikurs, Glasser). (3) **Behaviouristic/interventionist**: behaviour is learned; the teacher controls through reinforcement and consequences (Skinner, Canter).
>
> **(b)** Establishing clear **rules and routines** early; good **seating arrangement**; **withitness** and overlapping; smooth **transitions** and momentum; well-planned, engaging lessons; consistent **reinforcement**; positive teacher–pupil relationships.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Wolfgang & Glickman's continuum underlies the three models.

## Simplified explanation

Hands-off, shared, teacher-controlled.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: (a) State and explain **four** characteristics of **disadvantaged** pupils. (b) Describe **five** ways you can instruct disadvantaged pupils.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** (1) **Poor language development** and limited vocabulary; (2) **low self-esteem**/self-concept; (3) **poor health and nutrition**; (4) lack of **learning materials** and home support; (5) poor **attendance** and frequent dropout; (6) limited experiences and short attention span.
>
> **(b)** Use **concrete materials** and real-life examples; **individualised attention** and remedial lessons; generous **praise and encouragement**; involve parents/community; provide materials and a supportive environment; peer tutoring and group work.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Disadvantaged = deprived of the conditions that support normal development and learning.

## Simplified explanation

Poor language, low esteem, poor health; concrete, individual, encouraging teaching.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.
